title: A stored timestamp column records an instant, the same on every database
intent: A timestamp column declared without a timezone maps to a naive database type, which discards the zone of even a correctly-built aware value on the way in, so the moment a row records is ambiguous and ordering or comparison across zones is silently wrong. A column that keeps the zone on one database can still store the wall time on another, so the same row records a different instant depending on where it was written, and a test on one database proves nothing about the other. Every persisted timestamp column is declared with the framework's own timestamp type, which stores the instant as UTC on every database. This is the storage half of the hole whose in-memory half the naive-timestamp rule closes: capturing an aware value is worth nothing if the column cannot keep it.
reference: On a table model, a timestamp field (datetime, datetime | None, Optional[datetime], Union or Annotated around one, quoted or not) is refused unless the type that reaches its column is terp.core's UtcDateTime, called or as the class: the sa_type= value, or the type of sa_column=Column(...) (type_=, or its positional arguments, where the framework's type decides over a name given in a variable), with Column called by any name the file imports it under. A Field(...) inside Annotated is read the same way as one assigned. A type named anywhere else in the call does not reach the column and does not count. UtcDateTime counts imported from terp.core under any alias, or reached through the terp.core module (core.UtcDateTime, terp.core.UtcDateTime), resolved by the module's imports, definitions and assignments in source order up to the class, so a later import of another UtcDateTime wins. A UtcDateTime the file defines itself, imports from anywhere else, or reaches through a call's result is refused, since nothing holds it to storing UTC. DateTime(timezone=True) and TIMESTAMP(timezone=True), qualified or not, keep the zone on PostgreSQL and store the wall time on SQLite, so they are refused with the replacement named: the database column type is the same, so the change needs no migration (ADR 0205). A bare annotation, a Field() that never names the column type, and an explicit timezone=False are naive storage, and a column built elsewhere (sa_column=some_factory()) is refused as unreadable. Fields a table inherits from a mixin declared in the same file are in scope, since the column lands on the table either way. Classes no table inherits (DTOs, unrelated payloads) declare no columns, and migrations spell the column as the database sees it; both are out of scope.

runtime.rationale: Unlike the in-memory naive-timestamp rule — where the zone is already lost at the point the value is built, so no seam downstream can recover it — this invariant survives into the running system: the mapped column type is inspectable on the ORM metadata the framework already collects at boot, and a timestamp column whose mapped type is not UtcDateTime is decidable there without ambiguity. A fail-closed boot check over the collected table metadata would therefore add independent fidelity, catching a column whose naive type arrives from a path the source scan cannot follow: a dynamically built column, a mixin imported from another package, or a table contributed by an installed capability. The framework owns that seam (its create_app boot validations) but has not yet shipped this control.
runtime.tracking: terp-framework reference implementation: the create_app boot-validation seam in terp.core.app (alongside the existing _validate_* boot checks) — to walk the collected table metadata and refuse a timestamp column whose mapped type is not UtcDateTime.
